title: Review: Human gas exchange and ventilation; Gas exchange in fish, insects and plants; Circulatory systems and blood vessels; Tissue fluid and lymph; The heart and cardiac cycle
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Biology (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EX06#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX07#t3 term and clue written for the game; EX05#t4 term and clue written for the game; EX06#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EX02b#N.15a, EX03b#N.4, EX05#N.11, EX06#N.10, EX07#N.3, EX02b#N.2, EX05#N.18, EX06#N.5, EX07#N.6, EX05#N.8, EX07#N.14. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Lymph
items.clue: Excess liquid that has drained from around the cells into its own vessels

items.label: Diastole
items.clue: About 0.4 s in which all chambers relax and blood flows in from the veins

items.label: Capillaries
items.clue: Narrow vessels with a wall one cell thick, where flow is slowest and exchange occurs

items.label: Plasma
items.clue: The liquid part of blood, carrying dissolved substances and proteins such as albumin

questions.stem: At rest, an athlete's tidal volume is 0.6 dm³, inspiratory reserve volume 2.8 dm³ and expiratory reserve volume 1.4 dm³. During hard exercise her tidal volume rises to 2.2 dm³. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Her vital capacity rises to 6.4 dm³, because the extra tidal volume is added on to her resting volumes.
Her reserve volumes stay at 2.8 and 1.4 dm³, because the reserves are used only in a single maximal breath.
Vital capacity stays 4.8 dm³; the larger breaths leave reserves totalling 2.6 dm³.
The extra air comes from her residual volume, which can be breathed out only during exercise.

questions.stem: In a model of one gill lamella, water enters with a relative O₂ concentration of 100 and blood enters with 0. Water and blood flow at equal rates and carry O₂ equally well. What is the highest value the blood could reach with each type of flow?

options.text: 100 with parallel flow; 100 with counter-current flow
50 with parallel flow; 50 with counter-current flow
50 with parallel flow; close to 100 with counter-current flow
Close to 100 with parallel flow; 50 with counter-current flow

questions.explanation: Parallel flow stops at equilibrium, 50. Counter-current flow keeps a gradient all along, so blood approaches the 100 of incoming water.

questions.stem: A muscle receives blood through a network of thousands of capillaries rather than through a single vessel of the same total volume. What is the advantage of this arrangement for exchange?

options.text: A single wide vessel would have more wall area than thousands of narrow ones, so exchange inside it would be faster.
The narrow capillaries force the blood through faster, so more oxygen is delivered to the muscle each second.
Each capillary has fenestrations, which are needed so that cells can pass out of the blood into the muscle.
The total surface area of the many narrow, branching vessels is far larger, and all the blood is close to a wall.

questions.stem: Which statement describes how excess tissue fluid is drained and what happens to it?

options.text: It enters lymph ducts, which pump it along with their thick muscular walls to the kidneys, where it is excreted.
It stays in the lymphatic system as lymph, a separate fluid that circulates without rejoining the blood.
It is pushed back into the capillaries by the valves in the lymph ducts, which force fluid towards the blood.
It enters lymph ducts through gaps in their thin walls, valves prevent backflow, and the lymph is returned to the blood.

questions.explanation: The excess enters thin-walled lymph ducts through gaps; valves keep it moving one way; the ducts empty into veins.

questions.stem: The wall of the left ventricle is about three times thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Which statement correctly explains this difference?

options.text: The left ventricle pumps a larger volume of blood at each beat than the right ventricle, so it needs more muscle.
The left ventricle pumps blood to the lungs, which offer more resistance to flow than the rest of the body does.
The left ventricle must generate a much higher pressure to drive blood through the whole systemic circulation.
The left ventricle gets a stronger nerve impulse from the brain at each beat, so it has built up more muscle.

questions.stem: A student's spirometer readings are: tidal volume 0.5 dm³, inspiratory reserve volume 3.0 dm³, expiratory reserve volume 1.2 dm³. What is the student's vital capacity?

options.text: 4.2 dm³
4.7 dm³
3.5 dm³
1.7 dm³

questions.explanation: Vital capacity = tidal volume + inspiratory reserve + expiratory reserve = 0.5 + 3.0 + 1.2 = 4.7 dm³.

questions.stem: With age, the walls of large arteries lose elastic tissue and become stiffer. Blood pressure in an arm artery is measured at its highest (as the ventricle contracts) and its lowest (between beats). What change in these readings is expected?

options.text: The readings become steadier, because a stiff wall resists the surges better than a stretchy one.
The highest reading rises and the lowest falls: the swing in pressure gets bigger.
The lowest reading falls to zero, because nothing keeps blood under pressure between beats.
No change, because the muscle in the artery wall contracts with each beat to keep the pressure steady.

questions.stem: Blood pressure in a capillary is about 4.7 kPa at the arteriole end and about 1.3 kPa at the venule end. How do these values explain the release and reuptake of tissue fluid?

options.text: At 4.7 kPa blood pressure outweighs the osmotic pull of the plasma proteins, so fluid is forced out; at 1.3 kPa the pull is greater, so water moves back in.
Plasma diffuses out at the arteriole end because its concentration is higher there, and diffuses back in at the venule end where it is lower.
The pressure at the two ends is effectively the same, so fluid must be pumped back into the capillary by the venule.
The higher pressure at the arteriole end forces out blood cells and plasma proteins, which then return with the fluid at the venule end.

questions.stem: The sinoatrial node fires. Which sequence of events then follows in the left side of the heart?

options.text: The atrium and the ventricle contract at the same moment, and the atrioventricular and semilunar valves open together to let blood into the aorta.
The atrium contracts, filling the ventricle; the ventricle then contracts, shutting the atrioventricular valve and opening the semilunar valve; then both relax.
Muscles attached to the valves pull them open one after the other, and the ventricle contracts only after both valves have been opened.
A nerve impulse from the brain reaches the ventricle first, so the ventricle contracts and then the atrium contracts to refill it.

questions.explanation: Atrial systole completes ventricular filling. The ventricle's rising pressure shuts the AV valve and, once above aortic pressure, opens the semilunar valve. Diastole follows.

questions.stem: What is the role of the elastic tissue in the wall of an artery?

options.text: It contracts in waves behind the blood to push it along the artery towards the tissues.
It makes the wall stiff and rigid so that the high pressure cannot burst the artery.
It stretches during systole and recoils during diastole, maintaining pressure.
It forms flaps that actively open and shut to push blood forwards along the artery.

questions.explanation: Stretching during ventricular contraction stores energy; recoil returns it while the ventricle relaxes, keeping blood moving and pressure high between beats.

questions.stem: Pressures in the right side of a heart, early in ventricular systole: right atrium 0.4 kPa; right ventricle 1.0 kPa and rising; pulmonary artery 1.3 kPa. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The atrioventricular valve is open, because pressure in the ventricle is higher than in the atrium.
The semilunar valve is open, because the ventricle is contracting.
Both valves will open when the pacemaker sends a nerve signal to them.
Both valves are shut; the semilunar valve will open once ventricular pressure exceeds 1.3 kPa.

questions.explanation: Ventricle above atrium shuts the AV valve; ventricle below artery keeps the semilunar valve shut. As pressure keeps rising, it opens.
